topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 475.25(1)(a), F.S., makes it a ground for discipline for a broker to violate which of the following, while carving out one narrow exemption for real estate licensees?
choice_a: Any provision of Section 455.227(1), F.S. (DBPR's general disciplinary grounds) or Section 475.42, F.S. (real estate-specific violations) -- except licensees under Chapter 475 are exempt from Section 455.227(1)(i)
choice_b: Only violations of the federal Fair Housing Act, with no reference to any Florida statute
choice_c: Only violations of local county zoning ordinances
choice_d: Exclusively criminal statutes found outside Chapters 455 and 475, F.S.
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(a), F.S., provides: 'Has violated any provision of s. 455.227(1) or s. 475.42. However, licensees under this part are exempt from the provisions of s. 455.227(1)(i).' This structure incorporates both DBPR's cross-profession general disciplinary grounds and real estate-specific violations, with one narrow carve-out.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Separate from the general fraud/misrepresentation ground of Section 475.25(1)(b), F.S., Section 475.25(1)(c), F.S., makes it a distinct disciplinary violation for a broker to:
choice_a: Advertise property or services in a manner that is fraudulent, false, deceptive, or misleading in form or content
choice_b: Use a color scheme in print advertising that has not been pre-approved by FREC
choice_c: Include the licensee's own photograph in an advertisement
choice_d: Advertise a listing using a font size smaller than 10-point
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(c), F.S., provides that a licensee 'has advertised property or services in a manner which is fraudulent, false, deceptive, or misleading in form or content,' establishing false/misleading advertising as its own independent ground for discipline distinct from the general fraud provisions in paragraph (b).

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Under Section 475.25(1)(f), F.S., a broker's guilty plea or nolo contendere plea to a crime that directly relates to brokerage activities, or that involves moral turpitude or fraudulent/dishonest dealing, can support discipline even if:
choice_a: Adjudication was withheld by the court -- the statute applies 'regardless of adjudication'
choice_b: The plea occurred more than 50 years before the licensee applied for a real estate license
choice_c: The plea was entered in a foreign country with no U.S. treaty relationship
choice_d: The broker was acting under duress at the time of the underlying crime
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(f), F.S., applies to a qualifying conviction or plea 'regardless of adjudication,' meaning a withheld adjudication (common in plea agreements) does not shield the licensee from discipline based on the underlying plea or finding of guilt.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 475.25(1)(f), F.S.'s conviction-based discipline ground applies to a qualifying crime committed:
choice_a: In any jurisdiction, not only within Florida, so long as it directly relates to brokerage activities or involves moral turpitude or fraudulent/dishonest dealing
choice_b: Only within the State of Florida
choice_c: Only within the United States, excluding any foreign jurisdiction
choice_d: Only within the county where the broker's principal office is registered
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(f), F.S., reaches a conviction or qualifying plea entered 'in any jurisdiction,' so an out-of-state or even foreign criminal matter meeting the statute's relatedness/moral-turpitude/dishonesty standard can still support Florida license discipline.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 475.25(1)(h), F.S., makes it a discipline ground for a broker to:
choice_a: Share a commission with, or pay a fee or other compensation to, a person not properly licensed as a broker, broker associate, or sales associate, for referring real estate business or performing licensed real estate services
choice_b: Split a commission with another properly licensed Florida broker cooperating on the same transaction
choice_c: Charge a commission rate below the local market average
choice_d: Advertise the brokerage's commission rate on the firm's public website
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(h), F.S., prohibits sharing a commission or paying compensation to an unlicensed person for referrals or licensed real estate services -- a distinct violation from ordinary cooperative-commission splits between properly licensed brokers, which are lawful.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Beyond FREC's disciplinary guidelines treating a licensee's prior discipline as an aggravating factor in setting a penalty, Section 475.25(1)(o), F.S., separately establishes its own freestanding statutory ground for discipline based on:
choice_a: Being found guilty a second time of misconduct that warrants suspension, or a course of conduct showing incompetence, negligence, dishonesty, or untruthfulness
choice_b: A single instance of arriving late to one closing
choice_c: A broker's decision to specialize exclusively in one property type
choice_d: A broker's choice to work part-time rather than full-time in real estate
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(o), F.S., is itself an independent charging ground -- distinct from the disciplinary guidelines' treatment of prior discipline as an aggravating sentencing factor -- covering a second finding of suspension-level misconduct, or an established course of conduct demonstrating incompetence, negligence, dishonesty, or untruthfulness.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 475.25(1)(p), F.S., separately makes it a discipline ground for a licensee to fail to:
choice_a: Inform FREC in writing within 30 days after pleading guilty or nolo contendere to, or being convicted or found guilty of, any felony
choice_b: Inform FREC of a routine traffic citation within 24 hours
choice_c: Inform FREC of a change of personal cell phone carrier
choice_d: Inform FREC before taking a personal vacation of more than one week
explanation: Section 475.25(1)(p), F.S., independently penalizes a licensee's failure to notify FREC in writing within 30 days after pleading guilty or nolo contendere to, or being convicted or found guilty of, any felony -- a self-reporting duty distinct from the underlying conviction ground in paragraph (f).

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 475.25(5), F.S., generally requires an administrative complaint against a broker to be filed within:
choice_a: 5 years after the act giving rise to the complaint, or 5 years after the act is discovered or should have been discovered with the exercise of due diligence
choice_b: 6 months after the act, with no discovery-based extension available
choice_c: There is no time limit whatsoever for filing an administrative complaint
choice_d: 20 years after the act, matching Florida's general statute of repose for written contracts
explanation: Section 475.25(5), F.S., provides: 'An administrative complaint... shall be filed within 5 years after the time of the act giving rise to the complaint or within 5 years after the time the act is discovered or should have been discovered with the exercise of due diligence,' combining a standard limitations period with a discovery-rule extension.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: A broker commingled trust funds in 2018, but the misconduct was actively concealed and only discovered by a new office manager in 2024. Under Section 475.25(5), F.S., the 5-year deadline for DBPR to file an administrative complaint would generally run from:
choice_a: 2024, the date the act was discovered (or should have been discovered with due diligence), not merely the date the underlying act occurred
choice_b: 2018 only, with no discovery-based extension ever available
choice_c: The date the broker's license was originally issued, regardless of when the misconduct occurred
choice_d: There is no applicable filing deadline once any concealment is involved
explanation: Because Section 475.25(5), F.S., starts the 5-year clock from either the act itself or its discovery (whichever supports a later filing), concealed misconduct that is only later uncovered can still be timely charged if the complaint is filed within 5 years of that discovery.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Section 455.224, F.S., authorizes DBPR/FREC to resolve certain violations through a 'citation' process. This process is reserved, by rule, for violations that:
choice_a: Pose no substantial threat to the public health, safety, or welfare
choice_b: Resulted in a felony conviction of the licensee
choice_c: Involve any violation whatsoever, replacing the formal disciplinary complaint process entirely
choice_d: Were committed by a sitting FREC member
explanation: Section 455.224, F.S., directs boards and departments to adopt rules designating as 'citation violations' those violations 'for which there is no substantial threat to the public health, safety, and welfare' -- reserving the streamlined citation process for genuinely minor infractions.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: A broker who receives a citation under Section 455.224, F.S., and disagrees with it may, within 30 days after the citation is served:
choice_a: Dispute the matter and instead pursue the formal disciplinary procedure under Section 455.225, F.S.
choice_b: Take no action -- citations issued under Section 455.224, F.S., cannot be disputed under any circumstances
choice_c: Appeal directly and exclusively to the U.S. Supreme Court
choice_d: Automatically void the citation simply by ignoring it
explanation: Section 455.224, F.S., requires that a citation 'clearly state that the subject may choose, in lieu of accepting the citation, to follow the procedure under s. 455.225,' and that if the subject disputes the matter, the formal Section 455.225, F.S., procedures apply instead.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: If a broker fails to timely dispute a citation issued under Section 455.224, F.S., within 30 days after service:
choice_a: The citation becomes a final order of the department and constitutes discipline
choice_b: The citation is automatically voided and unenforceable
choice_c: The broker's license is automatically and permanently revoked
choice_d: The matter is automatically referred to a criminal grand jury
explanation: Section 455.224, F.S., provides that 'if the subject does not dispute the matter in the citation with the department within 30 days after the citation is served, the citation becomes a final order and constitutes discipline' -- an enforceable disciplinary action, not merely a warning.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: A citation issued under Section 455.224, F.S., differs from a letter of guidance issued in lieu of a probable cause finding in that:
choice_a: A citation imposes an actual penalty (such as a fine) for a minor violation and can become a final, binding disciplinary order, whereas a letter of guidance is a non-punitive corrective communication
choice_b: They are functionally identical, with no legal distinction between the two
choice_c: A letter of guidance is always more severe, automatically resulting in license suspension
choice_d: Only a letter of guidance can ever be reduced to a final order
explanation: A citation under Section 455.224, F.S., is itself a disciplinary penalty for minor violations (a fine, becoming a final order if undisputed), while a letter of guidance is a non-disciplinary, corrective measure issued instead of a probable cause finding -- the two tools serve different purposes at different stages.
source_note: Section 455.224, F.S.; Section 455.225, F.S. (letter of guidance)

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Under Section 455.224, F.S., a citation for a minor violation must generally be issued within:
choice_a: 6 months after the filing of the complaint that is the basis for the citation
choice_b: 24 hours after the complaint is filed
choice_c: 10 years after the complaint is filed
choice_d: There is no deadline for issuing a citation
explanation: Section 455.224, F.S., requires that 'a citation must be issued within 6 months after the filing of the complaint that is the basis for the citation,' giving DBPR a bounded window to use this streamlined enforcement tool.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Prior to a probable cause determination being made, records related to a pending complaint and investigation against a Florida broker are generally:
choice_a: Confidential and exempt from Florida's public records law
choice_b: Immediately posted on FREC's public website for consumer review
choice_c: Automatically forwarded to the broker's business competitors
choice_d: Available to any member of the public simply by informal request
explanation: Section 455.225(2), F.S., makes complaints and investigative records confidential and exempt from public disclosure while an investigation is pending, protecting both the integrity of the investigation and the licensee's reputation before any determination is made.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: A complaint and investigative file against a Florida broker generally becomes subject to public disclosure:
choice_a: 10 days after probable cause has been found by the probable cause panel or the department, or immediately if the licensee waives confidentiality -- whichever occurs first
choice_b: Only after the broker's license has been permanently revoked
choice_c: Immediately upon the complaint being filed, with no confidentiality period at all
choice_d: Never -- such records remain permanently sealed even after a final order is entered
explanation: Section 455.225(2), F.S., lifts the confidentiality exemption '10 days after probable cause has been found... or until the regulated professional or subject of the investigation waives his or her privilege of confidentiality, whichever occurs first,' setting a defined trigger for public access.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: If a probable cause panel fails to make its determination within the standard 30-day window under Section 455.225, F.S., what happens next?
choice_a: The department itself must make the probable cause determination within an additional 10 days after that time limit expires
choice_b: The complaint is automatically and permanently dismissed with prejudice
choice_c: The broker's license is automatically suspended pending further review
choice_d: The case is automatically escalated directly to a Florida circuit court jury trial
explanation: Section 455.225, F.S., provides a statutory backstop: if the panel misses the standard time limit, 'the department... must make a determination regarding the existence of probable cause within 10 days after the expiration of the time limit,' ensuring the case does not stall indefinitely.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Practicing as a broker or sales associate in Florida without a valid, active license, under Section 475.42(1)(a), F.S., is classified as which level of criminal offense?
choice_a: A felony of the third degree
choice_b: A non-criminal civil infraction carrying no criminal exposure
choice_c: A misdemeanor of the first degree at most
choice_d: A capital felony
explanation: Section 475.42(1)(a), F.S., prohibits operating as a broker or sales associate without a valid license, and a violation of this specific paragraph is classified as a felony of the third degree -- notably more severe than the general misdemeanor classification applied to most other Section 475.42 violations.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Aside from unlicensed practice under Section 475.42(1)(a), F.S. (a third-degree felony), most other violations enumerated in Section 475.42(1), F.S. -- such as making false statements to the commission or obstructing an investigation -- are generally classified as:
choice_a: A misdemeanor of the second degree
choice_b: A felony of the first degree, on par with armed robbery
choice_c: A purely civil violation carrying no criminal classification whatsoever
choice_d: A felony of the third degree, identical to unlicensed practice itself
explanation: While unlicensed practice under Section 475.42(1)(a), F.S., is singled out as a third-degree felony, the remaining violations listed in Section 475.42(1), F.S., are generally classified as a misdemeanor of the second degree -- a meaningfully lower criminal classification.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: Florida law permits DBPR to summarily suspend or restrict a broker's license on an emergency basis, ahead of the usual full disciplinary process, only when:
choice_a: The agency finds an immediate serious danger to the public health, safety, or welfare, documents specific supporting facts in writing, and promptly initiates a formal disciplinary proceeding thereafter
choice_b: Any single, uncorroborated complaint is received, regardless of its severity
choice_c: The broker has simply failed to pay an annual license renewal fee on time
choice_d: The FREC chair personally objects to the broker's advertising style
explanation: Emergency suspension or restriction of a license, under Section 120.60(6), F.S. (the Administrative Procedure Act), is permitted only where the agency finds an 'immediate serious danger to the public health, safety, or welfare,' supports that finding with written facts and reasoning, and follows up with prompt formal proceedings -- not for routine administrative lapses.

topic: Florida Law, FREC Rules & Disciplinary Process
question: For FREC to lawfully conduct official business at a meeting (such as voting on rules or ratifying disciplinary final orders), Florida's general quorum requirement for DBPR boards under Section 455.207, F.S., requires:
choice_a: 51 percent or more of the appointed members of the Commission to be present
choice_b: Unanimous attendance by all seven appointed members, with no exceptions
choice_c: Only a single member need be present, so long as that member is the chair
choice_d: A quorum is never required for any FREC business
explanation: Section 455.207, F.S., which applies generally to DBPR boards including FREC, provides that '51 percent or more of the appointed members of the board... shall constitute a quorum' -- a simple majority of the Commission's seven appointed seats.
